# Screw, nut and bolt (`screw_nut_bolt`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A screw is a slope wrapped round a cylinder. A single-start thread advances by one thread spacing (the pitch) per full turn, so a long handle and a fine pitch turn a small push into an enormous squeeze or a very fine adjustment: the principle of presses, vices, clamps, jacks and measuring instruments. To lay out a first screw, wrap a right-angled triangle of paper or thin metal round the rod and cut along its sloping edge; the nut is cast or cut to match. A screw and nut hold parts together and can be undone again, which nails and rivets cannot. Until threads are cut on a lathe to agreed sizes, every nut fits only its own bolt and they must be marked in pairs.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming screws were always around as fasteners; metal screws and nuts are rare before the 15th c. and costly until the 19th
  - A pitch so steep that the screw runs back under load
  - Mixing up nuts and bolts made by hand, or by different workshops
  - Assuming China had it; the screw was the one basic machine element absent there until the 17th c.
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – invention ascribed to Archytas (weak late tradition); 3rd c. BC water screw; 1st c. AD Hero describes screw presses and a tool for cutting internal threads; rome: 1st c. AD – screw presses for oil and wine, 'invented within the last hundred years' (Pliny, Natural History XVIII); small bronze screws in instruments; europe: 15th c. – metal screws in armour, clocks and presses; a screw-cutting lathe drawn in the Mittelalterliches Hausbuch (c. 1480); 1760 Wyatt brothers' screw-making machine; 1841 Whitworth proposes a standard thread; americas: 1864 – William Sellers's standard thread for the United States; china: 17th c. – screw introduced by the Jesuits
- Read:
  - Hero of Alexandria, Mechanica III (in A. G. Drachmann, The Mechanical Technology of Greek and Roman Antiquity, 1963)
  - Witold Rybczynski, One Good Turn: A Natural History of the Screwdriver and the Screw (2000)
